title: Exposure to natural disasters and vaccination indicators: a systematic review and directions for future research.
authors: Shea B, Shaman J
abstract: Global routine childhood immunization has stagnated for almost two decades, leaving children vulnerable to both immediate and long-term health risks from infectious diseases. Identifying and mitigating impediments to childhood vaccination, such as barriers resulting from exposure to natural disasters, is vital for maintaining population health. While there is general understanding that disasters have the potential to disrupt vaccination services, well designed studies on the degree to which exposure to natural disasters affects vaccination indicators are limited. Understanding the effects of natural disasters on vaccine preventable diseases is an important area for future research as some natural disasters are becoming more frequent and intense due to climate change. To understand the current state of research on exposure to natural disasters and vaccination indicators (i.e., vaccination metrics including administration, coverage, rates), we conducted a systematic literature review of all literature in Embase, Google Scholar, PubMed, and Web of Science up until September 11-12, 2025. We aimed to identify relevant peer reviewed literature focusing on natural disasters and immunization and to assess them for relevance and inclusion. Seventeen studies met the criteria for inclusion. These studies examined the relationship between exposure to cyclones/hurricanes, droughts, earthquakes, flooding, heat waves, and multiple disaster types and changes in vaccination among different age groups. Most (16/17 (94.12%)) papers identified a connection or association between exposure to natural disasters and reduced vaccination indicators. The majority (13/17 (76.47%)) of studies focused on early-childhood vaccinations. Characteristics that affect vulnerability to under-vaccination-exposure level, geographical location, socioeconomic status-were assessed in several papers. Areas for future research include quantifying the degree to which different disaster types affect multiple vaccination indicators within the same individuals and changes in communities over time.

title: Modern cell-based assays for biomedical research: from conventional methods to AI-driven high content analysis.
authors: Venkataramaiah C
abstract: In vitro cell-based assays are fundamental tools in biomedical research, supporting investigations of cellular physiology, disease mechanisms, drug discovery, toxicology, regenerative medicine, and precision therapeutics. However, conventional two-dimensional (2D) cell culture models often fail to recapitulate the structural complexity and physiological functions of native tissues, prompting the development of advanced platforms, including three-dimensional (3D) cultures, organoids, organ-on-a-chip technologies, and microphysiological systems. Recent advances in cell viability and cytotoxicity assessment, functional cellular analysis, molecular profiling, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based functional genomics, high-content imaging, flow cytometry, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and automated high-throughput screening have expanded the analytical capabilities of cell-based assays. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted image analysis and computational biology has enhanced cellular phenotyping, biomarker discovery, and mechanistic investigation, with the potential to improve the prediction of therapeutic efficacy and toxicity. Nevertheless, challenges related to physiological relevance, technical variability, inadequate standardization, high operational costs, scalability, poor reproducibility, cell-line misidentification, batch-to-batch variation, and inconsistent reporting continue to hinder translational applications. Future progress will depend on integrating physiologically relevant models with AI-driven analytics, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, automated screening, and microphysiological systems. Standardized protocols, harmonized reporting practices, and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to improve reproducibility, strengthen regulatory acceptance, advance precision medicine, and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. In this context, this review critically evaluates conventional and emerging in vitro cell-based assays, emphasizing their biological principles, analytical capabilities, translational applications, and practical limitations, while highlighting future opportunities to improve predictive accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical translation.

title: Artificial intelligence in antiviral drug discovery: Data resources, methods, and applications.
authors: You G, Li J, Chen J, Wang B, Xu Z, Wang J, Shang L
abstract: Viral infectious diseases remain a major global health burden, underscoring the urgent need for efficient strategies to identify novel antiviral agents, particularly those with broad-spectrum activity and a high barrier to resistance. With the rapid accumulation of diverse biological and chemical data, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into antiviral drug discovery to accelerate candidate identification and optimization. In this review, we summarize major data resources for AI-assisted antiviral research, including viral genome databases, viral protein databases, virus-host protein interaction databases, antiviral compound activity databases, compound structure databases, and viral mutation and drug resistance databases. We then review representative AI methods and applications across key tasks in antiviral drug discovery, including target-based drug discovery, phenotype-based drug discovery, and viral mutation and drug resistance prediction. We also summarize representative antiviral candidates from AI-assisted studies and their reported activities. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future opportunities in AI-assisted antiviral drug discovery. We believe that the continued advances in data resources and AI methodologies will accelerate the development of more effective antiviral agents.

title: Metal-organic framework-assisted signal amplification in electrochemiluminescent microRNA biosensing: Current advances and barriers to clinical implementation.
authors: Ren J, Cui H, Zhou X, Zhou X, Zhu Y, Wang J
abstract: The rapid expansion of electrochemiluminescence (ECL) biosensing has created growing demand for efficient signal amplification strategies capable of meeting the sensitivity requirements of microRNA analysis. Among the available functional materials, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have evolved from simple signal carriers into multifunctional platforms that integrate probe loading, catalytic enhancement, programmable nucleic acid reactions, and emerging CRISPR-assisted amplification within a single sensing architecture. This review provides a mechanism-oriented perspective on MOF-assisted signal amplification strategies, highlighting how different amplification mechanisms govern analytical performance and practical applicability. Beyond summarizing representative biosensing systems, the advantages, limitations, and suitable application scenarios of different amplification strategies are critically compared to establish guidelines for rational biosensor design. Finally, the remaining obstacles to clinical translation are discussed, together with future opportunities for developing robust, integrated, and clinically deployable MOF-based ECL biosensing platforms.

title: Fractionated Ablative Lasers: Principles, Parameters, Clinical Technique, and Complication Management.
authors: Leake D, Shah A
journal: Facial plastic surgery clinics of North America
abstract: Fractionated laser resurfacing for cutaneous rejuvenation delivers tightly controlled columns of thermal injury while preserving intervening tissue for rapid re-epithelialization. Compared to ablative lasers, fractionated lasers have decreased postoperative recovery, prolonged erythema, risk of pigmentary changes, and scarring. This article will focus on the basic principles of fractioned lasers, skin anatomy with relation to laser resurfacing, types of lasers, preoperative, perioperative and postoperative management, and mitigating and treating complications.

title: New and Emerging Infectious Diseases: Policy Trends.
authors: ShamaeiZadeh P, Khalfalla T, Westby S, Freeman EE
abstract: This article examines the evolving public health policy landscape surrounding new and emerging dermatological infectious diseases, and the evolving role of dermatology in global health surveillance. Throughout history, globalization, climate change, migrant and refugee displacement, stigmatization, workforce challenges, and health systems innovations have all influenced the detection and prevention of dermatological infectious diseases. Dermatologists have, and continue to, serve a unique role in contributing to global surveillance and in establishing a landscape for recent developments of global health initiatives, such as the World Health Organization resolution on Skin Diseases as a Global Public Health Priority.

title: Spectroscopic and structural characterization of human amniotic membrane after washing with plasma-activated water.
authors: de Almeida FS, Calheiro GAT, do Nascimento JM, de Lima Cordeiro TB, Klausner V, Doria ACOC, Sant'Anna LB
journal: Spectrochimica acta. Part A, Molecular and biomolecular spectroscopy
abstract: The human amniotic membrane (AM) is widely used in regenerative medicine; however, tissue processing and sterilization procedures may compromise its structural integrity. Plasma-activated water (PAW) has emerged as a potential alternative for tissue decontamination. This study evaluated the effects of PAW washing on the structural and molecular characteristics of human AM using histological and Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy analyses. AM fragments were divided into two groups: a PAW group, washed with plasma-activated water, and an antibiotic group (ATB), washed with penicillin, streptomycin, and amphotericin B. Following treatment, the fragments were cryopreserved and subsequently evaluated by histology and FTIR spectroscopy. Histological analysis revealed no apparent differences between the groups. FTIR analysis showed differences in band intensity in the amide III region on both membrane surfaces, while an additional difference at 1743 cm-1 was observed on the mesenchymal layer. Hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) of the 1400-1700 cm-1 spectral region showed high similarity between the PAW and ATB groups. Principal component analysis (PCA) primarily separated samples according to membrane surface rather than treatment. Overall, PAW washing did not induce detectable histological or molecular alterations in human AM compared with conventional antibiotic washing.

title: A portable smartphone-integrated chiral molecularly imprinted electrochemical sensing platform based on L-histidine-functionalized Q-HKUST/PEDOT for highly selective detection of L-tyrosine.
authors: Yu J, Zhang X, Han S, Wang Y, Chu H, Zong W, Leng Q
abstract: l-tyrosine (L-Tyr) is an important amino acid closely associated with human metabolism and neurophysiological functions. Abnormal L-Tyr levels are related to multiple physiological disorders, so accurate detection of L-Tyr in food is of great practical value. This study proposes a novel molecularly imprinted electrochemical sensor (MIP/PEDOT/Q-HKUST-His/SPCE) based on poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) and l-histidine (L-His)-grafted metal-organic framework (Q-HKUST-His) for the detection of L-Tyr. Q-HKUST-His with chiral centers and the conductive polymer PEDOT were sequentially modified on the surface of a screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE) to accelerate electron transfer, increase the effective surface area of the electrode, and facilitate the electropolymerization of molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs). The electrosynthesized MIPs significantly improved the selective recognition and enrichment of L-Tyr. The constructed MIP/PEDOT/Q-HKUST-His/SPCE (MPS) sensor exhibited a wide linear range (0.001-200 μmol L-1) and a low detection limit (0.116 nmol L-1). It also showed excellent selectivity for L-Tyr, with recovery rates of 98.64-104.62%. When coupled with a portable electrochemical workstation and smartphone-based data acquisition system, the proposed sensor enabled sensitive, accurate, and rapid on-site detection of L-Tyr in various food samples.

title: A genetic engineering toolkit for the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii.
authors: Dong H, Xiao C, Zhang Y
abstract: Saccharomyces boulardii (S. boulardii) is the only yeast probiotic widely used in clinical practice and consumer products. It combines gastrointestinal robustness, intrinsic antibiotic tolerance and eukaryotic protein-processing capacity, making it an attractive chassis for engineered probiotics, in situ biomanufacturing and live biotherapeutic delivery. However, host-specific characterization of regulatory elements, candidate genomic integration sites, and multicopy integration strategies remains limited in the clinically used S. boulardii CNCM I-745 background. Here, using S. boulardii CNCM I-745 as the host, we developed and characterized a genetic engineering toolkit that integrates transcriptional control elements with genome-integration strategies. We first quantified the activities of 20 endogenous constitutive promoters, two inducible promoters and six terminators. We then established a markerless CRISPR-Cas9 workflow and evaluated 10 chromosomal integration loci; six of which showed Editing efficiency above 80% while supporting comparable transgene expression without detectable growth penalties. Finally, we constructed an rDNA-repeat-based multicopy integration system that increased transgene expression by 9.8- to 22.6-fold relative to single-copy integration and revealed a significant positive but non-proportional association between estimated copy number and reporter output. Together, this toolkit provides S. boulardii with a set of tunable promoters and terminators, candidate chromosomal integration sites compatible with a markerless CRISPR-Cas9 workflow. These resources expand the genetic accessibility of this probiotic yeast and provide a foundation for developing engineered S. boulardii strains with enhanced probiotic, therapeutic and biomanufacturing functions.

title: Unlocking genetic accessibility in Halomonas bluephagenesis: A high-efficiency transformation chassis enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing.
authors: Xu T, Guo F, Xiang H, Han J
abstract: Halomonas bluephagenesis has emerged as a promising chassis for industrial biotechnology distinguished by its halophilic robustness and capacity for open and continuous fermentation. However, its poor transformability has substantially limited rapid, iterative, and automatable strain engineering. Here, we develop a "restriction release" strategy that increases transformation efficiency from approximately 102 to 107 cfu/μg DNA, rivaling the efficiency of standard laboratory Escherichia coli. A spontaneous IS30 insertion disrupting the type II restriction endonuclease gene notI increased plasmid transformation efficiency by about 2000-fold. Targeted deletion of notI reproduced this phenotype, confirming its role as a major barrier. Further deletion of the DNA phosphorothioation restriction locus dptFGH yielded an additional 10 to 37-fold improvement, generating the highly transformable ΔEPSΔFlgΔNotIΔPTRes chassis. Notably, the enhanced chassis further facilitated two linear-DNA-based editing strategies: direct RecET-mediated pyrF deletion using a linear donor coupled with phenotypic selection, achieving a recombination efficiency of 16.7%, and CRISPR/Cas9-assisted ribDHBA promoter replacement via co-delivery of a gRNA plasmid and a linear donor, achieving an efficiency of 11.1%. Together, these results identify endogenous restriction systems as primary barriers to genetic manipulation in H. bluephagenesis. Stepwise restriction release markedly improves plasmid transformation and enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing, providing an improved genetic platform for the iterative engineering of this industrial halophile. More broadly, this study suggests a practical strategy for overcoming the genetic inaccessibility of other non-model microorganisms and accelerating iterative strain engineering.

title: A background-suppressed CRISPR/Cas13a-HRCA biosensor for ultrasensitive miR-137 detection toward differential screening of Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Song J, Yue H, Zhang C, Jiao J, Jiao J
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with pathological changes that can occur years before the onset of clinical symptoms, highlighting the importance of sensitive biomarker detection for early diagnosis. Here, we developed a fluorescence biosensing platform based on CRISPR/Cas13a-assisted hyperbranched rolling circle amplification (CRISPR/Cas13a-HRCA) for the detection of the AD-related biomarker miR-137. A duplex composed of Linear-Bio and a Cas13a linker strand was first immobilized on streptavidin-coated magnetic beads to construct magnetic probes. In the presence of miR-137, the linker strand was displaced and released into solution through strand exchange and magnetic separation. The released linker activated the CRISPR/Cas13a system via complementary pairing with crRNA, leading to cleavage of the UUU site within the topological DNA reporter (TDR). The cleaved TDR subsequently initiated the HRCA reaction in the presence of Vent DNA polymerase and the P2 probe, generating abundant double-stranded DNA products for fluorescence readout using SYBR Green I. By combining CRISPR/Cas13a amplification, magnetic separation, and label-free fluorescence detection, the platform produced a fluorescence response to miR-137 over 10 fM-100 nM, with an LOD and LOQ of 1.77 and 11.11 fM, respectively. Recoveries ranged from 99% to 106%, with RSDs of 2.2-2.6% in aCSF. Furthermore, the method successfully distinguished cerebrospinal fluid samples from AD patients and healthy individuals, demonstrating its potential for AD-related miRNA analysis.

title: Transcription factor-regulated rolling circle transcription cascaded with Cas12a for sensitive determination of tetracycline.
authors: Chen S, Wang R, Su Y, Zhang J, Li Z, Xie S, Du Z, Liu J
abstract: The ability to perform convenient and user-friendly quantitative analysis of antibiotic residues in water is critical for mitigating ecological risks, yet current methods often suffer from limited sensitivity, fixed detection ranges, or complex procedures. Here, we present a hierarchical cascade signal amplification platform integrating rolling circle transcription (RCT) with CRISPR-Cas12a for one-pot tetracycline (Tc) detection. A rationally designed circular DNA template containing a T7 promoter, a TetR-binding motif, and a crRNA-encoding sequence serves as the molecular switch. In the absence of Tc, TetR binds to the template and blocks transcription. Upon Tc addition, TetR detaches, triggering RCT to produce numerous crRNA copies, which activate Cas12a-mediated trans-cleavage of fluorescent reporters, generating amplified signals. By adjusting the TetR-to-template ratio from 10:1 to 15:1, the detection range can be tuned from 6.0-100 nM to 20-600 nM, with detection limits of 1.35 nM and 16.4 nM, respectively. The system exhibits excellent selectivity against common interferents and achieves satisfactory recoveries (90%-110%) in spiked aquaculture tailwater, with results consistent with HPLC analysis. This platform offers hierarchical signal amplification, one-pot operation, tunable dynamic range, and modular template design, providing a versatile strategy for environmental pollutant monitoring.

title: Engineering a PEG/Co-modified carbon paste electrode for highly sensitive voltammetric determination of ophthalmic antihistamine epinastine: From pharmaceutical analysis to ocular pharmacokinetics.
authors: Al-Khateeb LA, Gamal M, Hussein OG
abstract: Rapid and highly sensitive monitoring of epinastine in pharmaceutical formulations and biological matrices remains a significant analytical challenge, demanding methods that combine simplicity, affordability, and excellent analytical performance. In this study, a polyethylene glycol/cobalt-modified carbon paste electrode (PEG/Co/CPE) was fabricated as a novel electrochemical sensing platform for epinastine determination. The combined incorporation of PEG and Co enhanced the electrochemical response through increased electrochemically accessible surface area and modified interfacial characteristics while scan-rate studies indicated predominantly diffusion-controlled epinastine oxidation. Following systematic optimization of the experimental conditions, the proposed square wave voltammetric method exhibited two linear concentration ranges of 20.0-1400.0 nM and 2.0-100.0 μM with excellent correlation coefficients (r = 0.9998 and 0.9997, respectively). The sensor demonstrated remarkable sensitivity achieving a limit of detection of 6.5 nM and a limit of quantification of 19.8 nM. Method validation confirmed excellent analytical reliability with recoveries of 99.84 ± 0.71% and 100.26 ± 0.65% while repeatability and intermediate precision showed relative standard deviation values below 1.5%. The method was successfully applied to the determination of epinastine in a commercial ophthalmic formulation affording a recovery of 99.72 ± 0.58% whereas the standard-addition procedure yielded a mean recovery of 99.85 ± 0.11% indicating negligible matrix interference. In rabbit aqueous humor, the bioanalytical assay displayed linearity over 20.0-1400.0 nM with r = 0.9998, a detection limit of 6.3 nM, and a quantification limit of 19.1 nM while satisfying accepted criteria for accuracy, precision, and stability. Furthermore, the validated sensor enabled successful pharmacokinetic profiling following ocular administration providing reliable estimates of Cmax (27.20 ng/mL), Tmax (4.0 h), and elimination half-life (5.59 h). Collectively, the developed sensor provides a robust, cost-effective, and high-performance electroanalytical platform with strong potential for routine pharmaceutical quality control and bioanalytical pharmacokinetic applications.

title: Multi-Loop Traction Device-Assisted Papillary Traction During Single-Balloon Enteroscopy-Assisted Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography After Roux-en-Y Gastrectomy: A Four-Case Series.
authors: Hirata D, Komoto S, Horiuchi T, Yoshioka M, Takahashi S, Furuhashi H, Narimatsu K, Hokari R
abstract: Biliary cannulation during single-balloon enteroscopy-assisted endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography after Roux-en-Y gastrectomy can remain challenging even after the papilla is reached. Unfavorable papillary orientation, tangential visualization, and excessive papillary mobility can impair alignment with the bile duct axis. We used a multi-loop traction device (MLTD; Boston Scientific Japan, Tokyo, Japan) as an adjunct for papillary traction in four patients with Roux-en-Y anatomy after gastrectomy. The indications were suspected distal bile duct cancer in one patient and common bile duct stones in three patients. An SIF-H290S enteroscope (Olympus Medical Systems Corp., Tokyo, Japan) was used in all patients. After MLTD traction, biliary cannulation and the intended diagnostic or therapeutic intervention were completed in all four cases. No procedure-related adverse events were observed during hospitalization or through the first outpatient visit after discharge. Traction corrected the papillary axis in papillae facing the blind limb and stabilized highly mobile papillae. MLTD-assisted papillary traction may serve as a practical rescue technique when difficult cannulation results from unfavorable papillary orientation or excessive mobility.

title: Simiao pill ameliorates collagen-induced arthritis in association with gut-joint axis modulation and attenuation of cGAS-STING signaling.
authors: Li T, Yang Y, Li G, Han L, Shen P, Ba X, Lin W, Yan J
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Simiao Pill formula (SM), composed of Phellodendron chinense C.K.Schneid., Atractylodes lancea (Thunb.) DC., Achyranthes bidentata Blume, and Coix lacryma-jobi var. ma-yuen (Rom.Caill.) Stapf, is a traditional Chinese herbal formula historically used for damp-heat Bi syndrome and commonly applied to the management of rheumatoid arthritis (RA)-related arthralgia symptoms. However, its anti-arthritic mechanisms remain incompletely defined. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study evaluated the anti-arthritic effects of SM in collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) and examined whether these effects were associated with gut-joint axis-related alterations and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A CIA mouse model was established and treated with SM for 6 weeks. Arthritis severity, joint pathology, bone erosion, serum cytokines, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, colonic histology, and tight junction proteins were assessed. Gut microbiota and colonic content metabolites were analyzed using 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. cGAS-STING pathway proteins were examined in joint and colonic tissues. A separate antibiotic-induced microbiota perturbation cohort was used to assess the contribution of gut microbiota to high-dose SM (SM-H) efficacy. RESULTS: SM reduced arthritis scores and spleen index in CIA mice. It decreased serum IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ levels, increased IL-10 production, and alleviated synovitis, cartilage damage, and bone erosion. SM also improved colonic histological abnormalities, enhanced colonic ZO-1 and Occludin expression, and reduced serum lipopolysaccharide-binding protein levels, suggesting improvement of intestinal barrier-related indicators. Gut microbiota and metabolomics analyses showed that SM-H reshaped gut microbial composition and colonic content metabolic profiles, particularly involving aromatic amino acid and vitamin-related metabolism. Correlation analysis linked representative microbial taxa and metabolites with arthritis severity, inflammatory responses, intestinal barrier markers, and bone parameters. Moreover, SM suppressed cGAS-STING pathway activation in both joint and colonic tissues. Under antibiotic exposure, the anti-arthritic, barrier-related, and cGAS-STING-inhibitory responses associated with SM-H were attenuated. CONCLUSIONS: SM ameliorated CIA in association with coordinated changes in gut microbial composition, colonic content metabolism, intestinal barrier-related indicators, systemic inflammation, and cGAS-STING signaling. Antibiotic exposure attenuated multiple SM-H-associated responses, supporting a contribution of microbiota-associated processes to the therapeutic response, although microbiota-specific causality was not established.

title: Siwu Paste alleviates blood deficiency syndrome induced by cyclophosphamide and acetylphenylhydrazine in association with gut microbiota remodeling and improved splenic metabolic homeostasis.
authors: Wan D, Feng X, Xu S, Du Q, Yue W, Zhang S
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Siwu Paste (SWP), derived from the classical blood-tonifying formula Siwu Decoction, has long been used for blood deficiency-related disorders and has a well-established traditional basis and ethnopharmacological value. Blood deficiency syndrome (BDS) is a common syndrome in traditional Chinese medicine and is associated with impaired blood generation and hematopoietic dysfunction. However, the modern pharmacological mechanisms underlying the beneficial effects of SWP on BDS remain incompletely understood. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aims to evaluate the therapeutic effects of SWP on cyclophosphamide and acetylphenylhydrazine induced BDS and to investigate the potential mechanisms underlying its improvement of hematopoietic function. METHODS: The chemical constituents of SWP were characterized by ultra-performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC-Q-TOF-MS), and its potential mechanisms were predicted using network pharmacology. An acetylphenylhydrazine (APH)/cyclophosphamide (CTX)-induced BDS rat model was used to evaluate SWP efficacy through flow cytometry, histology, Western blotting, qPCR, 16S rRNA sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), and exogenous adenosine diphosphate (ADP) supplementation experiments were performed to evaluate the contribution of the gut microbiota and the involvement of splenic ADP-related metabolic alterations. RESULTS: SWP significantly improved hematopoietic dysfunction, alleviated systemic inflammation, restored intestinal barrier integrity, reversed the Treg/Th17 imbalance, and reduced apoptosis within the CD45+CD34+ bone marrow cell population in BDS rats. Multi-omics analysis revealed that SWP significantly regulated gut microbiota composition and metabolic profiles; specifically, SWP treatment was associated with a significant increase in the relative abundance of Allobaculum and an upward trend in Lactobacillus, accompanied by a significant reduction in the relative abundance of total ADP in spleen tissue compared with the BDS group. FMT experiments partially transferred the hematopoietic and immunomodulatory effects associated with SWP treatment. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment and exogenous ADP supplementation attenuated several SWP-induced improvements in bone-marrow hematopoietic function and Treg/Th17 balance, consistent with the involvement of the gut microbiota-splenic metabolic axis in the therapeutic effects of SWP. CONCLUSION: SWP alleviates bone marrow hematopoietic dysfunction in BDS rats, with these effects accompanied by gut microbiota remodeling, restoration of intestinal barrier integrity, suppression of inflammation, and improved metabolic homeostasis. These findings provide modern pharmacological evidence supporting the traditional TCM concept of "treating the marrow via the gut" in blood deficiency-related disorders.

title: Xinlikang capsule ameliorates cancer-related fatigue in Lewis lung carcinoma tumor-bearing mice: association with inhibition of oxidative stress and attenuation of JNK activation and bone marrow apoptosis.
authors: Lu X, Huang S, Zhang Y, Ma T, Wang J, Wu X, Lv G, Wang F
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Cisplatin (DDP)-exacerbated cancer-related fatigue (CRF) and myelosuppression impair patients' quality of life, and effective interventions remain limited. Xinlikang Capsule (XLK), a proprietary Chinese medicine used as adjunctive oncology therapy, has unclear effects on CRF. AIM OF THE STUDY: To investigate the effects of XLK on CRF in Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) tumor-bearing mice and explore its mechanisms. MATERIALS AND METHODS: LLC tumor-bearing mice received control, model, DDP, or DDP plus XLK low-, medium-, and high-dose treatments. Fatigue behaviors, blood counts, bone marrow histology, and bone marrow cell populations were assessed. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) measured hematopoietic factors and cytokines. Network pharmacology predicted core targets, and apoptosis, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and JNK/NF-κB signaling were evaluated by histological, flow cytometric, immunofluorescence, and Western blot. RESULTS: XLK ameliorated fatigue-like behaviors, ncreased blood counts, improved marrow histology, elevated bone marrow cell populations, and modulated serum levels of hematopoietic factors and cytokines. Network pharmacology indicated apoptosis as a key pathway. XLK reduced bone marrow cell apoptosis and oxidative stress, restored mitochondrial function, downregulated apoptosis-related proteins (p-MKK4/7, p-JNK, Bax, and cleaved caspase-3), upregulated Bcl-2, inhibited NF-κB p65/IκBα phosphorylation, and reduced the co-localization of p-JNK and cleaved caspase-3. CONCLUSION: XLK alleviates DDP-exacerbated CRF and myelosuppression in LLC tumor-bearing mice. These effects are associated with suppressing of oxidative stress, restoring of mitochondrial function, attenuation of JNK activation, reduction of bone marrow apoptosis, and concomitant inhibition of NF-κB. However, direct causal validation of JNK signaling was not performed.

title: Isolation and characterization of rabbit intramuscular preadipocytes: Establishing a foundation for studies of intramuscular fat metabolism.
authors: Ahamba IS, Song G, Kinkpe L, Duan Q, Goswami N, Jin Z, Wu J, Dong X
abstract: Intramuscular fat (IMF) significantly influences meat quality, affecting flavor, tenderness, and juiciness. Despite extensive research on livestock such as cattle and pigs, the regulation of IMF in rabbits remains poorly understood. This study establishes a standardized in vitro method for isolating and characterizing intramuscular preadipocytes from the longissimus dorsi muscle of 3-day-old Hycole rabbits using enzymatic digestion and differential centrifugation. Three-day-old neonates were selected for initial protocol development due to their higher progenitor cell abundance and tissue accessibility, which facilitates method optimization and ensures consistent cell yields. Isolated cells displayed typical preadipocyte morphology and expressed key markers, including PREF-1, PPARγ, and Leptin, confirmed by RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence. Upon adipogenic induction, cells exhibited progressive lipid accumulation, as indicated by Oil Red O staining, and showed upregulated expression of PPARG, C/EBPa, and FABP4, confirming their differentiation potential. This study establishes a comprehensive protocol for isolating rabbit intramuscular preadipocytes, providing a foundational tool for investigating the molecular mechanisms of adipogenesis in lagomorphs. The model supports future studies on genetic and nutritional strategies to enhance rabbit meat quality while preserving its lean characteristics.

title: Modular engineering of aromatic metabolism in Corynebacterium glutamicum enables protocatechuic acid and gallic acid production.
authors: Pei J, Huang Q, Zhang B, Chu X, Wu X, Guo X, Ye B, Zhang B
abstract: Protocatechuic acid (PCA) and gallic acid (GA) are valuable phenolic compounds with diverse pharmacological activities, including antioxidant and antitumor properties, and have broad applications in the food, cosmetic, chemical, and pharmaceutical industries. However, the industrial production of these compounds remains limited by the insufficient performance of current microbial cell factories, resulting in low productivity and high manufacturing costs. Here, an efficient biosynthetic platform based on Corynebacterium glutamicum was systematically established for the production of PCA and GA. Through reconstruction of the PCA biosynthetic pathway, elimination of competing branches in the shikimate pathway, enhancement of the key rate-limiting enzyme, and modulation of the glucose uptake system to increase phosphoenolpyruvate supply, metabolic flux was effectively redirected toward PCA accumulation, resulting in the engineered strain PCA16 achieving a PCA titer of 19.8 g/L in shake-flask fermentation. Building on this platform, GA biosynthesis was established by introducing a mutant pobA from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and further strengthening the shikimate pathway, enabling strain GA06 to produce 7.86 g/L GA in shake-flask fermentation. Upon scale-up in a 5 L bioreactor, GA production was further increased to 25.66 g/L, representing the highest reported titer for GA production using C. glutamicum to date. Overall, this work demonstrates the strong potential of C. glutamicum as a robust microbial chassis for efficient production of PCA and GA, and provides a versatile platform for the biosynthesis of PCA-derived aromatic compounds.

title: Engineered microorganisms drive local metabolic reprogramming to Re-educate systemic immunity.
authors: Ma Y, Yang Y, Yu Z, Jin M, Jin Y, Wang J, Wang H, Zhao Q
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) features chronic synovial inflammation and systemic immune disorders. Current treatments mainly rely on systemic immunosuppression, raising risks of infection and long-term immune injury. Local therapies reduce such risks but struggle to regulate systemic immunity. Emerging studies show the synovial immunometabolic microenvironment links local inflammation to systemic responses. Here, we developed a strategy based on chemically attenuated photosynthetic bacteria that couples lactate metabolism with photo-driven hydrogen production to achieve local metabolic reprogramming and systemic immune re-education. We screened a photosynthetic bacterial strain with high lactate metabolic capacity, which also exhibited enhanced hydrogen production. To ensure safety, bacteria were PEGylated to mask immunogenic moieties while preserving metabolic activity. Intra-articular injection disrupted pathological crosstalk and restored the Treg/Th17 balance locally. Circulating IL-6 levels decreased, restoring the systemic regulatory role of Tregs, thereby alleviating distant joint inflammation. These results demonstrate that local synovial metabolic reprogramming by engineered bacteria can induce systemic immune re-education, offering a conceptually new therapeutic strategy for treating autoimmune arthritis.

title: Dual-zone swelling microneedle-smartphone platform for simultaneous colorimetric quantification of glucose and pH in diabetic wound interstitial fluid.
authors: Zhou Y, Li S, He L, Qi L, Yin G, Zhou H, Long W, Chen Y
abstract: Diabetic wounds undergo dynamic changes in local metabolism and infection-associated microenvironments, making timely assessment of wound status challenging. Herein, we report, to the best of our knowledge, the first dual-zone swelling microneedle-smartphone platform for simultaneous colorimetric quantification of glucose and pH directly from diabetic wound interstitial fluid (ISF). The platform combines a swelling microneedle patch, termed "IDB-CMN", with a companion WeChat mini program, "IDB-CMN Insight". Two spatially separated response zones are incorporated into the patch, using a glucose oxidase-horseradish peroxidase-3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbenzidine (GOx-HRP-TMB) cascade for glucose detection and m-cresol purple (mCP) for pH sensing. After local ISF uptake, the resulting colorimetric responses are analyzed by IDB-CMN Insight, which extracts RGB values from user-selected regions and converts them into quantitative glucose concentrations and pH values using pre-established calibration equations. The patch exhibited a mechanical strength of approximately 0.4 N per needle and a maximum swelling ratio of approximately 305%, with quantitative response ranges of 0.5-5.0 mg mL-1 for glucose and pH 6.0-10.0. In non-infected and Staphylococcus aureus-infected diabetic mouse wounds, the platform captured temporal changes in local glucose and pH that were consistent with conventional measurements, while infected wounds maintained a more alkaline microenvironment. Concurrent analysis of these two parameters provides complementary information on local metabolic and infection-associated changes and may offer early indications of adverse microenvironmental shifts during wound healing, supporting future risk assessment and treatment optimization.

Qi Yin San Liang San prevents gefitinib-induced nociceptive hypersensitivity by modulating TRPV1 channel activity.
authors: Yan K, Guo PX, Liang QY, Xu PT, Jin T, Chen LY, Liang CB, Guo MY
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Qi Yin San Liang San (QYSLS) is a traditional Chinese medicine formula used as an adjunctive therapy for malignant tumors, and has been reported to reduce treatment-related toxicities. Gefitinib-associated nociceptive hypersensitivity remains underrecognized, with its underlying causal mechanism poorly defined. It is unclear whether QYSLS can prevent gefitinib-evoked adverse effect and the underlying molecular mechanism remain unknown. AIM OF THE STUDY: To explore the molecular mechanism of gefitinib-provoked nociceptive hypersensitivity and evaluate the preventive effects of QYSLS, with specific investigation of TRPV1 channel activity and CGRP release from dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neuron under this pathological condition. METHODS: A mouse model of gefitinib-provoked nociceptive hypersensitivity was established. QYSLS protection was assessed via pain behavioral tests and DRG histopathology. RNA-seq and network pharmacology were used for target screening. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR), cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) and molecular docking confirmed direct gefitinib-TRPV1 binding. Calcium imaging evaluated TRPV1 channel activity in primary DRG neurons and TRPV1-overexpressing cells. Trpv1-/- mice were used to validate its function. RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence staining and ELISA measured DRG TRPV1/CGRP expression and CGRP release. RESULTS: Gefitinib induced time-dependent declines in mechanical withdrawal thresholds (8.7% of the control at day 28) and thermal withdrawal latencies (55.3% of control at day 28), accompanied by DRG injury in mice. DRG RNA-seq revealed elevated Trpv1 transcripts levels and enrichment of ion channel pathways. Gefitinib triggered TRPV1-dependent elevation of intracellular Ca2+ signals in DRG nociceptive neurons. Calcium imaging, SPR, CETSA, molecular docking and site-directed mutagenesis showed that gefitinib directly activates TRPV1. Residue Y454 is critical for this effect, while it is dispensable for capsaicin-mediated TRPV1 activation, and this activation elicits significant Ca2+ influx, neuronal excitation, and increased CGRP in DRG neurons. Genetic deletion of Trpv1 largely restored pain thresholds and rescued gefitinib-caused neuropathic pain. Oral QYSLS alleviated gefitinib-evoked weight loss, DRG histological damage and nociceptive hypersensitivity (recovered to 50.5% of control for mechanical withdrawal thresholds, and 94.7% of control for thermal withdrawal latency at day 28), accompanied by reductions in gefitinib-triggered DRG TRPV1 and CGRP expression of ∼34.6% and ∼56.1%, respectively. Quercetin and ferulic acid, the key bioactive ingredients of QYSLS, can inhibit gefitinib-induced TRPV1 activation. The analgesic-protective effects of QYSLS were substantially blunted in Trpv1-/- mice. CONCLUSIONS: This work identifies a previously unrecognized mechanism: Gefitinib triggers nociceptive hypersensitivity via DRG TRPV1 direct activation. Residue Y454 is critical for gefitinib- but not capsaicin-evoked TRPV1 activation, and CGRP may act as a downstream effector. QYSLS prevents this nociceptive hypersensitivity largely through TRPV1.

title: Ethnopharmacological basis of Huangqin Tang in colorectal cancer: Repurposing a classical formula to overcome PD-1 resistance via lactylation blockade.
authors: Song L, Zhang X, Liu A, Li X, Chen P, Liu X, Zeng A
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Huangqin Tang (HQT), documented in the Shanghan Lun, is traditionally prescribed for "dysenteric disorders" (Li Ji). Modern clinical studies confirm its efficacy against ulcerative colitis and colorectal cancer-associated inflammation, providing a verified traditional basis for investigating its immunomodulatory effects in colorectal malignancy. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to investigate the regulatory role of lactate-induced protein lactylation in MIF-driven PD-1 resistance and to determine if HQT can reverse this phenotype through metabolic reprogramming. MATERIALS AND METHODS: CT26-bearing BALB/c mice were administered HQT intragastrically combined with intraperitoneal anti-PD-1 antibodies. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes were profiled by flow cytometry. Integrative transcriptomics and network pharmacology were utilized to screen candidate targets. LC-MS/MS-based lactylomic profiling identified specific modification sites. Lactate modulation assays, and site-directed mutagenesis (NF-κB1 K249R) coupled with rescue experiments were performed in vitro to validate the molecular cascade mechanistically. RESULTS: HQT synergized with anti-PD-1 to suppress tumor growth and prolong survival. This combination remodeled the immune microenvironment, increasing CD8+ T cells and M1-like macrophages while reducing M2 macrophages and MDSCs. Mechanistically, HQT inhibited tumor glycolysis and lactate production. Lactylomic analysis revealed that lactate induced NF-κB1 lysine 249 (K249) lactylation in CD4+ Tregs, driving MIF transcription. Introducing the K249R mutation abolished lactate-induced MIF expression and reversed immunosuppression. HQT effectively reduced NF-κB1 K249 lactylation, disrupting the MIF-driven feedback loop. CONCLUSION: NF-κB1 K249 lactylation acts as a critical post-translational switch linking tumor glycolysis to Treg-mediated immunosuppression. HQT overcomes PD-1 resistance by suppressing this axis. These findings support combining metabolic intervention with immunotherapy and highlight K249 lactylation as a potential biomarker for treatment response.

title: Exposure-informed deconstruction of Chaihu Shugan San links tetramethylpyrazine-paeoniflorin to PRKACA-related neurotrophic signaling and brain-gut pharmacology.
authors: Zhou R, Cai Z, Wang Y, Gao Z, Zhang H, Huang X
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Chaihu Shugan San (CSS) is traditionally used for emotional constraint and digestive discomfort. Identifying botanical and constituent contributions to these coordinated actions could clarify its pharmacological basis. AIM OF THE STUDY: To identify an active reduced CSS preparation and investigate its constituent contributions and PRKACA-related signaling. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Botanical screening and recombination were conducted in chronic unpredictable mild stress rats. The selected combination, FCP (Aurantii Fructus, Chuanxiong Rhizoma and Paeoniae Radix Alba), was chemically characterized. Tetramethylpyrazine (TMP) and paeoniflorin (PF) were measured in plasma after single-dose CSS administration and tested at FCP constituent-equivalent oral doses. Hippocampal assays, Prkaca silencing in HT22 cells and JMV2959 co-treatment examined molecular and pharmacological responses. RESULTS: FCP showed the broadest behavioral and gastrointestinal activity among the reduced preparations tested. TMP/PF reproduced selected FCP-associated responses and increased hippocampal cAMP, PKA activity, BDNF, PSD95 and Synapsin-1. Prkaca silencing attenuated cellular neurotrophic and synaptic-protein responses to TMP/PF. Compared with TMP/PF alone, JMV2959 co-treatment reduced gastric emptying, intestinal transit, sucrose preference and hippocampal cAMP, PKA activity and BDNF, whereas plasma acyl-ghrelin and open-field distance did not differ significantly. CONCLUSIONS: FCP retained coordinated behavioral and gastrointestinal actions of CSS, while TMP/PF reproduced a defined component of this pharmacology. Convergent cellular and hippocampal findings support PRKACA-related signaling as a mechanistically relevant component of the constituent response.

title: Dendrobium officinale extract ameliorates Alzheimer's disease by modulating PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway and autophagy-related processes: An integrated study combining feature-based molecular networking, network pharmacology and multi-omics.
authors: Fu J, Liang Z, Wang F, Xiong F, Wang X, Sun J, Zhan J, Hu K
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder with limited effective treatments. Dendrobium officinale Kimura & Migo (D. officinale) has been traditionally used for dementia, but its active constituents and mechanisms remain unclear. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to systematically characterize the chemical constituents of D. officinale extract (DOE) and elucidate its anti-AD mechanisms using an integrated pharmacological strategy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The chemical composition of DOE was analyzed using UHPLC-Q-TOF/MS combined with feature-based molecular networking (FBMN). Target prediction and pathway analysis were performed using a network pharmacology approach. Therapeutic effects were evaluated in 5×FAD mice using behavioral and histopathological assays. Mechanistic validation was further conducted using transcriptomics, proteomics, qRT-PCR, Western blotting, and molecular docking. RESULTS: Sixty-five components were identified, with apigenin, naringenin, rutin and oxyresveratrol as major identified constituents. Integrated multi-omics and network pharmacology analyses highlighted the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway and autophagy-related processes as potential mechanisms underlying the anti-AD effects of DOE. In 5×FAD mice, DOE markedly improved cognitive deficits, alleviated hippocampal neuronal injury, reduced Aβ plaque deposition, and suppressed astrocytic and microglial activation. Mechanistically, DOE significantly downregulated the mRNA expression of Pi3k, Akt, and Mtor, reduced AKT and mTOR phosphorylation, and showed a trend toward decreased PI3K phosphorylation. DOE also reduced p62 accumulation and increased the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, suggesting an improvement in autophagy-related processes. Molecular docking further demonstrated favorable binding affinities of major identified constituents toward key targets, particularly AKT1 and PIK3CA. CONCLUSION: DOE ameliorates AD-related pathological changes, potentially through modulation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway and improvement of autophagy-related processes. These findings provide experimental evidence supporting the potential of D. officinale as a multi-target therapeutic candidate for AD.

title: Cardioprotective effects of Xin-Shu-Ning tablets against myocardial ischemia: Involvement of protein kinase B-related signaling in apoptosis and pyroptosis.
authors: Liu Y, Liu X, Gu Y, Xu F, Chen Y, Su W, Ding S, Qian C
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Xin-Shu-Ning Tablets (XSNT) are traditionally used to promote blood circulation and resolve blood stasis, including for coronary heart disease-associated angina. Their cardioprotective mechanisms and bioactive constituents remain unclear. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to evaluate the cardioprotection of XSNT against myocardial ischemia and to investigate its underlying mechanisms and candidate bioactive constituents. MATERIALS AND METHODS: XSNT was evaluated in myocardial infarction (MI) mice using echocardiography, biochemical assays, histopathology, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence. Proteomics and prior network pharmacology guided PI3K/AKT analysis. H9c2 cells underwent 8 h of oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD), with MK-2206 used to assess AKT involvement. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, cellular thermal shift assays, and cellular experiments were used to evaluate the candidates. RESULTS: XSNT improved cardiac function and reduced myocardial injury in MI mice. Reduced TUNEL staining and changes in Bcl-2/Bax and cleaved caspase-3 supported attenuation of apoptosis, while reductions in inflammasome- and GSDMD-related proteins indicated decreased pyroptosis-related signaling. These effects accompanied increased AKT phosphorylation and reduced NF-κB activation. XSNT produced similar responses in OGD-challenged H9c2 cells, and MK-2206 partially attenuated these effects. Puerarin showed a potential interaction with AKT and reproduced some cellular effects of XSNT, which were also attenuated by MK-2206. CONCLUSION: XSNT attenuated myocardial injury and distinct apoptosis- and pyroptosis-related responses, with pharmacological evidence supporting AKT involvement. Puerarin represents a candidate bioactive constituent. This study has several limitations, including the unclear cellular sources of myocardial pyroptosis-related signals, the lack of genetic validation of AKT involvement, and the need for further confirmation in primary cardiomyocytes.

Oral and anal detection of Treponema pallidum DNA among transgender women and travestis with high-titre syphilis in Brazil: findings from the MyTTrA study.
authors: Salle R, McCartney DJ, Grange PA, Mee P, Costa S, Magno L, Berçot B, de Sousa Mascena Veras MA
abstract: BACKGROUND: Data on transgender women and travestis (TGW) concerning oral and anal detection of Treponema pallidum (TP) DNA are lacking. We aimed to estimate the prevalence of oral and anal TP DNA detection and the frequency of azithromycin resistance-associated mutations among TGW with high-titre syphilis in Brazil. METHODS: We conducted a nested cross-sectional study as part of the TransOdara study among TGW in five Brazilian cities. Participants with high-titre syphilis (reactive treponemal test and VDRL titre ≥1:8) and an analysable oral or anal specimen underwent quantitative PCR targeting the tpp47 and polA genes to detect TP DNA. TP DNA-positive specimens were further analysed using nested PCR and Sanger sequencing to identify mutations associated with azithromycin resistance. FINDINGS: Among the 249 participants with high-titre serological syphilis and analysable sample, TP DNA was detected in 25 (10.0%, 95% CI 6.6-14.5): 14 (5.6%) from the oral site only, 6 (2.4%) from the anal site only, and 5 (2.0%) from both sites. Participants in whom TP DNA was detected were younger and more frequently reported STI symptoms and anogenital ulcers during the preceding six months. The detection rate increased with VDRL titre (odds ratio 2.44, 95% CI 1.74-3.41 per doubling of titre for any oral or anal detection). Mutations associated with azithromycin resistance were observed in 76% (19/25, 95% CI 54.9-90.6) of participants in whom TP was detected. INTERPRETATION: TP DNA was detected in 10% of participants with high-titre serological syphilis. Detection increased with higher VDRL titres, supporting an association between higher non-treponemal titres and mucosal TP DNA detection. These findings support continued epidemiological and molecular surveillance of syphilis and of azithromycin resistance in transgender populations. They do not support site-specific PCR screening: syphilis diagnosis remains serological, and benzathine benzylpenicillin G remains the treatment of choice. FUNDING: French National Agency for Research on AIDS, Viral Hepatitis, and Emerging Infectious Diseases (ANRS/MIE).

title: From individual-based models to macroscopic dynamics of antimicrobial resistance.
authors: Menale M, Toscani G, Zanella M
abstract: We introduce and discuss a kinetic framework describing the time evolution of the statistical distributions of a population divided into the compartments of susceptible, infectious, recovered, and resistant in the presence of a microbial infection driven by susceptible-infectious interactions. Our main objective is to quantify the impact of excessive and inappropriate antimicrobial use, which accelerates the spread of resistance by enabling a fraction of infectious individuals to transition into the resistant compartment. The model consists of a system of Boltzmann-type equations capturing binary interactions between susceptible and infectious individuals, complemented by linear redistribution operators that represent recovery, the development of resistance, and reinfection processes. In the grazing-collision limit, we show that this Boltzmann system is well approximated by a system of coupled Fokker-Planck equations. This limiting description allows for a more tractable analysis of the dynamics, including the characterization of the long-time behavior of the population densities. Our analysis highlights how interaction terms drive the system toward a stable equilibrium and quantifies the effects of inappropriate antimicrobial use on the distribution of resistant individuals. Overall, the results offer a multi-scale perspective that bridges kinetic theory with classical epidemic modeling.
